# 2D Sprite Atlas & Hitbox Packer: Getting Started

Pack sprites into atlases and check their silhouettes, hitboxes, palettes and memory use on your target devices.

An atlas (or sprite sheet) is one large image that holds many small images, so the game loads and draws them together. A hitbox (or hit shape) is the invisible shape the game uses to decide what touches what: an attack, a platform under the player's feet, a pickup or the area a click or tap lands on. The template works for pixel art and for smooth high-resolution art, in 2D games and for the 2D icons and interface art of 3D games. Every example below is one case among several.

If `engine/lens.mjs`, `engine/lens-kit.mjs` or `fixtures/good-pack.json` are not on disk yet, write them byte for byte from the `sprite-hitbox-packer-lens-engine` skill first (Node 18+, no dependencies).

## 1. Onboard one question at a time

Ask one question at a time, wait for the answer, then ask the next. Never stack questions in one message. Give no setup steps until questions 2 and 3 are answered.

1. Which game are we reviewing? After the answer, ask for the build to review (a build ID, commit or version), then ask where the evidence will come from (a CI job, an export script or manual captures).
2. What kind of 2D art does the game use: pixel art scaled up with sharp pixels (nearest filtering), smooth high-resolution art (linear filtering, often with mipmaps, the smaller pre-shrunk copies of a texture), or both? This decides `atlasFilters`, `atlasMips` and how much padding the atlas needs.
3. Which engine or packing tool makes the atlases (for example Unity Sprite Atlas, Godot's atlas import, TexturePacker, an Aseprite export or a custom script)? Use only that route from now on, and do not install tools on your own.
4. Do sprites take part in gameplay collision: hits, the ground under the player in a platformer, pickups, or the area a click or tap lands on? If none do, we use the `no-hit-shapes` profile: both `hit-shape` lines read N/A and their 20 points are shared over the other eight lines. Skip question 5.
5. Does the game have a height or depth layer that changes what touches what? For example jumping over a hazard in a top-down game, a bridge over a road, lanes in a side-scrolling brawler, or two clickable objects stacked on screen. If not, we use the `no-height-layer` profile.
6. Does the game ship install icons (a web app manifest, mobile app icons or a desktop shortcut icon)? If not, we use the `no-install-icons` profile.
7. Are items, collectibles or medals told apart by colour tiers or rarity levels (for example common and rare loot, bronze, silver and gold medals, or crop quality stars)? If not, we use the `no-item-tiers` profile. If the game shows no item or collectible art at all, `reward-art:1` has no profile and stays U.
8. Which values go in your game profile (`pack.profile`)? Start from the synthetic profile in `fixtures/good-pack.json` and go through the keys in the table below one at a time. Confirm or replace each value; never keep a sample number without the owner saying so.
9. What is your texture budget per scene, and which install icon sizes do the platforms you ship to require?
10. Who reviews the local finding drafts?

| Profile key | What it means |
|---|---|
| `devices` | The devices or screen classes you capture, for example `desktop` and `phone`. |
| `minIconPx` | Smallest on-screen size, in pixels, at which icons are checked for readability and bleed (a coloured seam taken from a neighbouring image in the atlas). |
| `atlasSizes`, `atlasFilters`, `atlasMips` | Display sizes, filter modes (`nearest` for pixel art, `linear` for smooth art) and mip levels to test. Every combination with every device becomes one test case. |
| `minPaddingPx`, `minPackingOccupancy` | Empty border around each frame in the atlas, and how much of the atlas area frames should fill. These feed a growth check that is reported but not scored. |
| `requiredIconSizes` | Install icon sizes, in pixels, that your platforms require. |
| `maxTextureBytesPerScene` | Texture budget per scene, in bytes. |
| `minItemArtPx` | Smallest displayed size for reward, item or collectible art. |
| `maxTierPaletteDeltaE`, `minTierDeltaE` | Largest colour drift allowed between a tier's reference colour and what is drawn, and smallest colour difference required between two different tiers. DeltaE is a standard colour distance; about 2 is barely visible. |

Read the profiles you picked back to the owner and, once they approve, set them before scoring, for example `"rubricProfile": ["no-item-tiers", "no-install-icons"]` in `pack.profile`. A selected line reads N/A (not U, not a defect), its points move to the lines that still apply, and the verdict can reach PASS.

Before grading a real pack, check that its build and profile match what the owner chose. Record a capture or run that could not happen as NOT_RUN. Each line needs a sample population (the list of measured cases it reads); `node engine/lens.mjs --meta` lists them.

## 2. What you provide

- An evidence pack (JSON) with `status: "VALID"`, a `liveSha` (the build that was running when you captured), a `gitSha` (the source commit) and a `packId` (all three are required), and an `artifacts` list. Every metric group names the artifact id it came from.
- Metric groups this engine reads: `icons` (capture), `atlas` (capture), `install` (trace), `iconSet` (static), `itemArt` (capture), `tierPalette` (capture), `weight` (trace), `decode` (trace), `hitShape` (trace), `heightLayer` (capture), `packing` (trace).
- Profile thresholds in `pack.profile`. A missing threshold makes its line U, never a default.
- Anything you cannot capture yet stays out of the pack. It grades U (UNMEASURED), which is honest and costs no false defect. A line your game does not need reads N/A once its profile is approved; without a profile it stays U.

## 3. Run the first grade

```
node engine/lens.mjs fixtures/good-pack.json   # worked example, synthetic, not a measurement
node engine/lens.mjs your-pack.json            # your build
node engine/lens.mjs --meta                    # rubric lines, weights and what each reads
node engine/lens.mjs --fixtures fixtures/good-pack.json  # negative and missing-input self-test
```

Read the record: `verdict` (PASS, CONDITIONAL, BLOCKED or INVALID), `grade` and `coverage`, then each line's `level` and `findings`, then `checks` (growth checks reported beside the grade) and `tickets` (deduplicated candidates).

## 4. Report in plain English

- Lead with the verdict, grade and coverage in one sentence. Say how much of the rubric was measured.
- List U lines as "not measured yet" with the capture that would measure them. Never call them defects.
- One local ticket draft per measured finding, with the pack id and artifact ids. Label any synthetic pack as synthetic.
- Rubric lines: icons:1, icons:2, install-icons:1, install-icons:2, reward-art:1, reward-art:2, texture-weight:1, texture-weight:2, hit-shape:1, hit-shape:2.

## 5. Skills in this template

- `sprite-atlas-packer`: Pack sprites, icons or interface art into atlases with padding and extruded edges so filtering never bleeds, for pixel art or smooth art, and prove they render clean on every device.
- `sprite-hit-shape-checker`: Check the shapes the game uses to decide what touches what (attack hitboxes, platform collision, pickups, click or tap areas) against the code that really uses them, frame by frame.
- `sprite-palette-and-readability-checker`: Check that reward, item or collectible art reads at its displayed size and that colour tiers and palette swaps stay distinct and match the palette rules.
- `sprite-hitbox-packer-lens-engine`: the engine source and how to run it.

## Blockers to tell the owner about

- Icon readability needs device captures; the worked example is synthetic.

Before capture, agree on the test cases in `profile.cases`: one `atlasMatrix` case per device, size, filter and mip combination, one `frameColliders` case per frame and shape you check, and one `tierSeparation` case per pair of tiers. After capture, `receipts` holds one measured row per case with the case id, the `liveSha` of the build that ran, the artifact id and the measured values. Run `node engine/lens.mjs --meta` for the required row fields and comparisons. A skipped or stale case leaves its line U. The bundled rows and budgets are synthetic.

# Atlas packing without bleed

Bleed is a coloured seam that appears when the renderer samples pixels from a neighbouring image in the atlas. This skill packs frames tightly while keeping every frame clean. It feeds `icons:1`, `icons:2`, `texture-weight:1`, `texture-weight:2` and the `atlas-packing` growth check, and, if your game ships install icons, `install-icons:1` and `install-icons:2`.

## 0. Ask first

Ask which art style and which packing tool the project uses, then follow only that route. Do not install tools on your own; if the tool is missing, record NOT_RUN and ask the owner.

- Pixel art: nearest filtering, usually no mipmaps, scaled by whole numbers (2x, 3x) so pixels stay square. A 1 to 2 px extruded border is often enough, but the camera can still land between pixels, so keep padding.
- Smooth high-resolution art: linear filtering, often with mipmaps. Each mip level halves the padding, so a frame that must stay clean down to mip level n needs at least 2 to the power n pixels of padding. Use premultiplied alpha if your engine supports it, to avoid dark fringes on soft edges.
- Packing tools: Unity Sprite Atlas (padding setting), Godot's atlas import, TexturePacker, an Aseprite sheet export or your own script. Record the tool name and version.

## Method

1. Trim transparent borders from each frame, then hash the trimmed pixels; identical pixels can share one slot. Keep one manifest record per source frame with its frame ID, source size, trim offset, pivot, packed rectangle and rotation. Frames with identical pixels but different pivots must keep their own pivots.
2. Pack with a rectangle packer. MaxRects (a common algorithm that places each frame in the free rectangle it fits best; "best short side fit" is a good default) works well. Record occupancy as used area divided by atlas area (`packing.occupancy`).
3. Pad every frame and extrude its edge pixels into the padding (repeat the outermost row and column outward). Record `packing.paddingPx`.
4. Check every combination you ship: each device, display size, filter and mip level from the profile. Store one row per approved combination in `receipts.atlasMatrix` with its bleed pixel count from a capture zoomed to pixel level, and record `atlas.combosRequired`, `atlas.combosChecked` and `atlas.bleedFailures`.
5. Icons: capture each icon on its supported devices at its smallest displayed size (`icons.minDisplayedPx`) and count bleed pixels (`icons.bleedPixels`).
6. Weight: record texture bytes for each representative scene (`weight.bytesPerScene`), and confirm every referenced image resolves and decodes in a complete build (`decode.referenced`, `decode.decoded`, `decode.completeBuild`).

Short examples (synthetic, for illustration only):

- Pixel-art platformer: 16 px tiles at 3x scale, nearest filtering, no mips. A one-pixel seam between ground tiles shows when the camera scrolls.
- Mobile puzzle game: smooth 256 px gem sprites shown at 64 px with mipmaps. Padding too small makes a purple fringe at mip level 2.
- Card game: large card art in one atlas per set. Texture bytes per scene matter more than occupancy.
- Farming sim: two crop frames with identical pixels that sit at different heights in the field (different pivots). Store the pixels once, keep both pivots.
- 3D game interface: inventory and map icons in an atlas drawn with linear filtering at several screen scales.

## Install icons (only if your game ships them)

Install icons are the icons a platform shows outside the game: a web app manifest, a mobile app icon set or a desktop shortcut. If the game ships none, the owner approves the `no-install-icons` profile: both lines read N/A and their 20 points are shared over the other eight lines.

- Record the sizes present in the build (`iconSet.sizesPresent`) against `requiredIconSizes` in the profile.
- Check that every icon file or URL resolves and decodes in the running build (`install.urls`, `install.resolvedAndDecoded`).
- If the running build is older than the source and simply lacks a new icon, report that as the build lagging behind, not as a broken asset (`install.liveBehindSeparated`).

## Negative fixture

Pack one test atlas with padding 0 and confirm the bleed capture shows a seam and the check fails.

## Pitfalls

- Checking only the desktop build; phones often use a different scale and filter.
- Occupancy pushed so high that frames lose their padding.
- Rotated frames in the atlas without the runtime knowing they are rotated.

Gather evidence for `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>` (see `sprite-hitbox-packer-lens-engine`).

# Hit shape verification

A hit shape is the invisible box, circle or polygon the game uses to decide what touches what. Use this skill only if sprites in your game take part in gameplay collision; otherwise the owner approves the `no-hit-shapes` profile and both lines read N/A, never a defect. It feeds `hit-shape:1` and `hit-shape:2`.

## 0. Ask first

Ask which kinds of shapes the game uses, then check only those. Examples (synthetic, for illustration only):

- Platformer: the body box that stands on the ground and one-way platforms. A crouch frame may shrink it; a jump frame must not snag on ledges.
- Point-and-click adventure: hotspots on scene objects. A hotspot can be larger than the drawn object on purpose; the expected shape comes from the design, not the pixels.
- Mobile puzzle game: tap areas on pieces, often padded to a minimum touch size.
- Top-down RPG or farming sim: pickup and interaction areas (harvest a crop, open a chest, talk to a villager).
- Shoot 'em up: a player hitbox much smaller than the ship sprite.
- Fighting or action game: per frame, three shapes kept apart: hurt (where the character can be hit), push (keeps bodies from overlapping) and hit (the attack). Mixing them causes ghost hits and stuck bodies.

## Method

1. Trace the real caller. For each shape, find the gameplay code that actually reads it: damage, collision resolution, a pickup trigger or a click or tap hit test. Shapes drawn only by a debug or diagnostics overlay do not count (`hitShape.diagnosticsOnly` must be false). The engine expects `hitShape.tracedCaller` to be the fixed value `"gameplay-path"`, which means "traced to the gameplay code that really uses the shape". Use that value even when the code is a collision or click handler, and name the real function in the trace artifact.
2. Per animation frame, compare the frame and shape the gameplay code consumed with the exported frame manifest: frame ID, shape ID, pixel hash, pivot, source size, trim offset and rotation. Store one row per approved case in `receipts.frameColliders`. When frames share pixels after deduplication, they keep their own pivots.
3. Height or depth: if the game has a height or depth layer, list repro cases where two things sit at different heights or depths. For example jumping over a hazard in a top-down game, walking under a bridge, standing on a different lane in a side-scrolling brawler, or two clickable objects stacked on screen. Each case must resolve by the model the design declares (`heightLayer.reproCases`, `heightLayer.resolvedByDeclaredModel`). Without such a layer, the owner approves the `no-height-layer` profile and `hit-shape:2` reads N/A.
4. Capture a short clip of each repro before and after a fix.

## Negative fixture

In a test copy, move a shape onto the wrong frame and confirm the check fails.

## Pitfalls

- Shapes taken from a debug overlay instead of the gameplay code.
- Frame indexes shifted by one after an animation is trimmed.
- A click or tap area tested at desktop size only; touch screens may need a larger area.

Gather evidence for `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>` (see `sprite-hitbox-packer-lens-engine`). Features the game does not have (install icons, reward tiers, a height layer) read N/A under their approved profile (`no-install-icons`, `no-item-tiers`, `no-height-layer`), never as failures.

# Item art, colour tiers and palette check

Use this when the game shows reward, item or collectible art (loot, cards, medals, crops, stickers, unlocks), when items are told apart by colour tiers, or when sprites are recoloured by palette swaps. It feeds `reward-art:1` and `reward-art:2`. If it has no colour tiers, the owner approves the `no-item-tiers` profile and `reward-art:2` reads N/A. If the game has no such art at all, `reward-art:1` has no profile and stays U. N/A and U are never defects.

## 0. Ask first

Ask which of these the game has, then check only those. Examples (synthetic, for illustration only):

- Action RPG or looter: common, rare and epic item frames.
- Card game: card rarity gems on the card border.
- Sports or racing game: bronze, silver and gold medals or trophies.
- Farming sim: crop quality stars in three colours.
- Mobile puzzle game: booster icons in a shop strip.
- Pixel-art game with palette swaps: one enemy sprite recoloured for each region.

## Method

1. Readability: render each item icon at the size the interface actually shows it on each device (`itemArt.minDisplayedPx`, `itemArt.unreadable`). Check it with the real filter setting; icons that look fine in an atlas preview often blur after mipmapping.
2. Colour drift: pair each approved reference colour with the colour actually drawn for that tier (`tierPalette.pairs`) and compare the largest difference with `maxTierPaletteDeltaE`.
3. Tier separation: measure the colour difference between each pair of distinct tiers in `receipts.tierSeparation` and compare it with `minTierDeltaE`. Review the tiers under simulated colour blindness as well. A tier must also read from shape, icon or label, not colour alone.
4. Palette swaps: if you recolour sprites with a lookup table (a LUT, a small image that maps each source colour to a new one), check the swapped output against the palette rules, not the source art.
5. Lit sprites: if sprites use normal maps for lighting, check that the apparent light direction does not flip between frames.

## Negative fixture

Change one drawn colour far from its reference and confirm the drift check fails. For the tier check, bring two distinct tiers close together and verify the separation check fails while their shape or label still tells them apart.

## Pitfalls

- Thresholds (`maxTierPaletteDeltaE`, `minTierDeltaE`, `minItemArtPx`) come from your profile, not from this skill.
- Checking tiers on a desktop monitor only; phone screens shift colours.

Gather evidence for `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>` (see `sprite-hitbox-packer-lens-engine`).

ENGINE: the lens engine is embedded in the sprite-hitbox-packer-lens-engine skill. Write both files byte for byte before the first run. Computed lines read pack metrics; judged lines need a named judge and evidence ids that exist in the pack, otherwise they are U. Computed lines trust pack.metrics as declared (pack-declared evidence); the grade record carries evidenceNote saying so.

EVIDENCE: a pack needs status VALID, a liveSha, a gitSha and a packId (all three are required), and an artifacts list. Metric groups read: icons, atlas, install, iconSet, itemArt, rarity, weight, decode, hitShape, elevation, packing. Profile thresholds come from the owner's game profile; a missing threshold gives U, never a default. Check the sample populations listed by the engine in --meta. Empty evidence earns U. Approved profiles no-hit-shapes (both hit-shape lines), no-height-layer (hit-shape:2), no-install-icons (both install-icons lines) and no-item-tiers (reward-art:2): the owner approves them before scoring and sets rubricProfile in the game profile; those lines read N/A, their points move to the lines that still apply, the verdict can reach PASS and the report names the profiles. A missing feature with no profile, such as no item art at all for reward-art:1, stays U and is never a defect. hitShape.tracedCaller must be the fixed value gameplay-path, meaning traced to the real gameplay code even when that code handles collision, pickups or clicks.

ONBOARDING: ask one question at a time. Before giving setup steps, ask whether the art is pixel art (nearest filtering) or smooth high-resolution art (linear filtering, often with mipmaps) and which engine or packing tool makes the atlases. Ask, one per message, which features the game has: gameplay hit shapes (if not, the no-hit-shapes profile), a height or depth layer (if not, no-height-layer), install icons (if not, no-install-icons), item colour tiers (if not, no-item-tiers). The owner approves each profile before scoring. Settle early: the texture budget per scene and the install icon sizes the platforms require.

HOUSE RULES: use the frame-time and response targets for each supported device from the game profile. No en or em dashes. Write the game's full name. Credit @meta_alchemist. Label every worked example synthetic and never invent a measurement.

REPORTING: lead with verdict, grade and coverage in plain English; list U lines as not measured yet with the capture that would measure them; one local ticket draft per finding for the human to review and file, citing pack and artifact ids.
BLOCKERS: Icon readability needs device captures; the worked example is synthetic.

Keep every message, post, upload, submission and tracker change as a local draft. Only the human reviews and sends, publishes, uploads or files it. Work only on a working branch. Push only when the human asks and only to that branch. Never push to main. The human merges and deploys. Any feature switch you add is off by default.

TEAM: this is gbf-17-sprite-hitbox-packer version 1.0.1, team spec 1.0.0. Before acting, read inputs from .grokbot-team/artifacts/<artifact>/ (game-profile (required), evidence-pack (required), feel-findings, fairness-findings) and memory topics decisions, releases from .grokbot-team/memory/. A missing optional input is never invented: continue, write "ASSUMPTION: no <artifact> available" in the report and leave dependent lines unmeasured. Save outputs (atlas-manifest, grade-record, ticket-draft) as local files for human review. Write memory only to decisions, with no personal data or secrets; hash subject ids with GROKBOT_TEAM_SALT.

routines.description: Draft a local weekly grade and evidence comparison for human review.
routines.content: Use the owner-approved pack for the intended build and profile. If capture or execution is unavailable, record NOT_RUN locally. Run `node engine/lens.mjs <pack.json>`. Draft a local report with verdict, grade, supported points, coverage, interval (the lowest and highest grade possible once the U lines are measured) and U lines. Record both build IDs and rubric hashes. Compare levels only for matching rubric hashes and profiles, and explain the cause of each change. Draft one local ticket candidate per measured finding with its pack and artifact IDs for human review. Only the human files or sends drafts. Work only on a working branch. Push only when the human asks and only to that branch. Never push to main. The human merges and deploys. Any feature switch you add is off by default.
